title: Connoisseurship: the expert eye and its limits
summary: What the trained eye does well, how it has failed, and why a good opinion states its confidence.

shots.title:
The expert eye —
and its blind spots.
shots.narration: Connoisseurship is the trained eye: years of looking, until an artist's hand becomes recognisable. It is indispensable — and it has failed spectacularly.
Morelli's habit-spotting grew into a discipline. Its grandest project, the Rembrandt Research Project, ended its final volume in 2014 by asking: what is a Rembrandt, and what is not?

shots.text: **Autograph**, workshop, follower: the eye grades authorship.
shots.narration: The eye's output is a graded attribution: autograph, by the master's own hand; then workshop, follower, imitator. Each grade is a judgement, not a measurement.

shots.text: Experts hailed the Emmaus as **Vermeer's masterpiece**.
shots.narration: The eye's failures are famous. Leading Dutch experts hailed Van Meegeren's Emmaus as Vermeer's masterpiece, while a curator who doubted another of his fakes kept his verdict to a private diary.

shots.text: Hofstede de Groot backed his eye **against the chemistry**.
shots.narration: Hofstede de Groot backed his eye against chemical proof of modern materials. Confidence is not evidence.

The answer isn't to abandon the eye. The National Gallery's exhibition 'Close Examination' showed scientists, conservators and art historians together telling originals from workshop pieces, copies and fakes.
Use each tool for what it does well. The eye spots a weak hand and an implausible composition. It cannot date a pigment, and it is vulnerable to wanting a discovery to be true.

shots.text: Courts want **yes or no**. Evidence gives probabilities.
shots.narration: One more pressure: in court, experts are pushed to answer authentic or not, when the evidence supports only degrees of probability. Good reports state their confidence.

steps.title: Go deeper: Revisiting Rembrandt
steps.caption: A Metropolitan Museum of Art programme of case histories in connoisseurship: how Rembrandt attributions have been made and revised (about 70 minutes).

steps.title: Strong evidence, or weak on its own?
steps.brief: An attribution report lists the following. Which are strong evidence of who painted it, and which are weak on their own?

cards.text: A signature in the right place
cards.why: A signature is the easiest thing to add — and one painted on top of the varnish shows dark under UV.

cards.text: A certificate from a famous expert
cards.why: Certificates record opinions, and experts' stamps have been forged.

cards.text: Materials all consistent with the claimed date
cards.why: It shows the work could be old, not who made it.

cards.text: A face that closely resembles one in a famous work by the master
cards.why: Painters of a period shared ideals of beauty; resemblance is not authorship.

cards.text: An underdrawing and changes of mind typical of the master's working process
cards.why: Pentimenti and drawing habits record how the picture was made, and help attribution.

cards.text: An unbroken chain of inventories back to the artist's studio
cards.why: Independent documents tied to the object are the backbone of attribution.

questions.prompt: What does 'autograph' mean in an attribution?
options: Painted entirely by the named artist
questions.explain: Autograph means by the artist's own hand, rather than partly or wholly by assistants.

questions.prompt: What did the Emmaus affair show about expert consensus?
options: Consensus can be wrong, and doubts may go unvoiced
questions.explain: Leading experts hailed a fake as a masterpiece; at least one doubter kept quiet.

questions.prompt: Why should an authentication report state its confidence?
options: Evidence usually supports degrees of probability, not certainty
questions.explain: Courts often want yes or no, but honest reports say how sure they are and why.

steps.title: Looking journal: the connoisseur's comparison
steps.brief: Find two works given to the same artist in a museum's online collection — one catalogued 'by' the artist, one 'attributed to' or 'studio of'. Compare them as a connoisseur would.

fields.label: Compare the handling — drawing, modelling, small details. Does the difference in grading convince you?
